# Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models

Yumeng Zhang    Zhengbang Yang    Yevin Nikhel Goonatilake    Zhuangdi
Zhu Affiliation: George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA

###### Abstract

Distilling reasoning traces from strong large language models into
smaller ones is a promising route to improve intelligence in
resource-constrained settings. Existing approaches face a fundamental
trade-off: offline distillation from teacher-generated traces provides
high-quality, sample-efficient supervision but suffers from
distributional drift: during training, the student model conditions on
teacher-generated prefixes, whereas during inference the student
autoregresses on self-generated prefixes, leading to compounding errors
over long reasoning trajectories. Meanwhile, on-policy or
self-distillation methods better match the student’s inference-time
distribution, but require costly online sampling and often produce
low-quality traces in early training. We propose a principled offline
reasoning distillation framework that preserves the efficiency and
supervision quality of offline teacher-generated data while correcting
teacher–student distribution drift. It adaptively emphasizes teacher
supervision that is better aligned with the student’s on-policy
distribution. Evaluations on mathematical reasoning benchmarks of GSM8K,
MATH, MATH500, and harder held-out competition-style tasks, including
AMC, AIME, and OlympiadBench, show that our method improves reasoning
accuracy over prior offline distillation algorithms and yields more
stable reasoning traces while preserving instruction-following
capabilities. Our work shows that lightweight,
distribution-correction-aware training can substantially strengthen
offline reasoning distillation without online rollouts.¹¹ 1 Code is
available at
[https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Discord-E6BC](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Discord-E6BC).

## 1 Introduction

Reasoning ability has emerged as a cornerstone of modern large language
models (LLMs), largely driven by scaled model architecture and advances
in reinforcement learning (RL)-based post-training optimization. This
capability is particularly important in scientific and engineering
domains such as mathematics, robotics, and physics, where solving
problems requires structured, multi-step reasoning instead of
short-horizon token prediction. Despite these advances, high-quality
reasoning behavior is still primarily observed in large or proprietary
models. Enabling smaller models to acquire similar reasoning ability is
critical for practical deployment, especially in resource-constrained
environments where efficient and reliable intelligence is required. The
ability to transfer reasoning competence across models without
significant performance degradation is crucial.

A common approach to reasoning distillation is to train a smaller
student model on reasoning traces generated by a stronger teacher model.
In this paradigm, referred to as offline learning or behavior cloning,
training data are collected from an external model. In contrast,
on-policy methods generate data from the target model itself and update
the model using policy-gradient RL techniques such as GRPO
\[[30](#bib.bib30)\] or token-level extensions \[[21](#bib.bib21),
[42](#bib.bib42), [46](#bib.bib46), [43](#bib.bib43)\].

Offline distillation offers several advantages. It is typically more
sample-efficient, and teacher-generated trajectories provide
higher-quality supervision, especially during early stages of training.
However, it also faces the inherent limitation of distribution drift:
the distribution of teacher-generated trajectories differs from the
distribution induced by the student model during inference. As the
student generates intermediate tokens that deviate from teacher
trajectories, it enters support regions that are underrepresented in the
training data. This distribution shift leads to compounding errors and
unreliable behavior. Existing approaches alleviate this issue through
refined distillation objectives, such as bidirectional divergence
minimization \[[17](#bib.bib17)\], but these methods do not directly
resolve the distribution mismatch, where the optimization is still
focused on a teacher-provided distribution.

We propose a principled method for LLM reasoning distillation that
relies solely on offline, teacher-provided data while reducing the
distribution gap to on-policy training. We first design a general
reasoning-eliciting instruction that contextualizes a large teacher
model to produce high-quality reasoning traces. These traces serve as
supervision for training a smaller student model. We then introduce a
distribution-corrected objective that incorporates an advantage-based
weighting mechanism, enabling the student to better align with
trajectories it is likely to encounter during inference. Our formulation
provides an effective approach for reducing the teacher–student
distributional drift and is compatible with most offline distillation
frameworks. We focus on mathematical reasoning as a representative
domain. Empirical results across multiple models and math benchmarks
demonstrate that our method consistently improves the reasoning
performance of student models in both in-domain and out-of-domain
settings, outperforming existing offline distillation baselines and
narrowing the gap to that of online sampling methods without requiring
online interaction.

## 2 Preliminary

#### On-policy Learning.

On-policy methods, especially on-policy RL, have been widely adopted for
LLM post-training in domains such as math reasoning and safety
alignment. The core idea behind this approach is to fine-tune a
pretrained model $`\pi_{\theta}`$ to maximize accumulated rewards within
a domain $`\mathcal{Q}`$ over self-generated trajectories:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
J_{\text{RL}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{Q},\;y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\mathds{R}(y,x)\right],
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\mathds{R}(x,y)`$ is a reward function that scores a response
$`y`$ (e.g., a reasoning trajectory). Following the policy gradient
principle \[[32](#bib.bib32)\], we derive the following gradient update
for
Eq. ([1](#S2.E1 "In On-policy Learning. ‣ 2 Preliminary ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{RL}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{Q},\;\underbrace{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}_{\text{On-policy sampling}}}\left[\mathds{R}(x,y)\cdot\sum_{t=0}^{|y|}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,\,y_{:<t})\right],
``` |  | (2) |

Prior work has improved training stability by replacing the reward
function $`\mathds{R}(x,y)`$ with a normalized Advantage function,
tokenizing the optimization formulation, and introducing clipping and
model update constraints \[[30](#bib.bib30), [7](#bib.bib7),
[21](#bib.bib21), [42](#bib.bib42), [46](#bib.bib46),
[43](#bib.bib43)\].

A key advantage of this strategy over supervised fine-tuning (SFT) lies
in its on-policy learning: the data used to optimize the target model is
sampled from itself instead of from another behavior policy. It
mitigates distribution drift, where the model encounters
underrepresented regions at inference time, and often benefits
out-of-domain generalization.

However, online methods are costly in terms of sample collection and
labeling, requiring a notably higher number of training samples than
supervised fine-tuning, and each trajectory requires labeled rewards.
Additionally, for smaller LLMs, the sample quality is also limited by
the model’s own capability, which leads to rare high-return trajectories
and slow asymptotic convergence.

#### Offline Knowledge Distillation.

A parallel path towards improving pretrained LLM performance is
knowledge distillation from another stronger model, such as an advanced
teacher LLM $`\pi_{T}`$. One straightforward method is to directly
perform SFT on teacher-generated reasoning traces, which trains the
target (student) model $`\pi_{\theta}`$ to imitate teacher behavior by
maximizing the log-likelihood of teacher-generated responses:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
J_{\text{SFT}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{Q},\;\underbrace{y\sim\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x)}_{\text{off-line sampling}}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{|y|}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,\,y_{:<t})\right].
``` |  | (3) |

Here the expectation is taken under the teacher distribution
$`\pi_{T}`$, with $`y`$ drawn from an offline dataset provided by the
teacher model. This behavior-cloning style method is training- and
sampling-efficient but is also prone to performance drop induced by
distribution drift, since this offline objective does not directly
optimize the target ($`\pi_{\theta}`$) model’s performance when $`y`$ is
sampled from $`\pi_{\theta}`$ during inference.

Subsequent methods supervise the student model with more refined teacher
signals, often by minimizing a distributional divergence between the
teacher and student models, such as the KL-divergence:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle J_{\text{KD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{Q},\;y\sim\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{T}(y|x)|\pi_{\theta}(y|x))\right].`$ |  | (4) |

Works along this line include optimizing on a reverse KL divergence
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{T})`$ \[[4](#bib.bib4)\] or
a mixture of both directions \[[17](#bib.bib17)\]. While these
algorithms show empirical performance improvement over direct SFT, they
still inherit a fundamental limitation of offline data: the training
objective provides a biased signal for the student’s on-policy behavior.
At inference time, the student model may generate prefixes that are
underrepresented in the offline teacher data, leading to unreliable
behavior \[[1](#bib.bib1)\].

![Refer to caption](2605.14071v1/figures/overview.png)

Figure 1: Overview of DisCorD: Standard offline distillation imitates
fixed teacher traces under teacher-generated prefixes, but during
inference the student conditions on its own prefixes, causing
distribution drift and compounding errors (left). DisCorD reduces this
mismatch by reweighting offline teacher-token supervision according to
the student’s support, emphasizing teacher behaviors that are more
reachable under the student’s inference-time distribution (right).

## 3 Methodology: Distribution Corrected Distillation from Offline Data

In this paper, we aim to improve cross-model knowledge distillation for
reasoning, where a teacher LLM with more advanced reasoning ability
provides supervision for a student LLM. To elicit strong teacher
behavior, we first design a reasoning instruction as a conditional
context $`c`$ when sampling traces from the teacher:
$`y\sim\pi_{T}(x;c)`$, which forms an offline reasoning dataset for
student distillation.

Our goal is to retain the data-efficiency benefits of offline
distillation while reducing the distributional gap between
teacher-generated traces and the student’s on-policy behavior. The core
idea is to introduce a student-support-aware correction that reweights a
training trajectory $`\{x,y\sim\pi_{T}(x;c)\}`$ with a density ratio
$`\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\bar{\pi}_{T}(y\mid x;c)}`$, where
$`\bar{\pi}`$ denotes a stop-gradient operation.

#### Stabilized Transformation.

However, directly applying such a density ratio leads to high training
instability, as the density ratio is unbounded and accumulates high
variance over long sequences. We address this in two steps. First, to
obtain a bounded and monotonic approximation, we apply a sigmoid
transformation to the log density ratio:
$`r(y\mid x)=\sigma\!\left(\tau\cdot\log\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\bar{\pi}_{T}(y\mid x;c)}\right),`$
with a temperature coefficient $`\tau`$ set to 1 by default. It
monotonically preserves the ordering induced by the density ratio while
mapping the correction into a bounded range of $`(0,1)`$.

Meanwhile, directly applying $`r(y\mid x)`$ as a sequence-level weight
still introduces length bias, where longer trajectories can accumulate
larger aggregate log-probability differences that inflate their
correction weights. To mitigate such length bias and variance, we apply
token-level approximation, following a strategy that has also been
adopted to stabilize RL training \[[45](#bib.bib45)\]. Specifically, we
tokenize the correction by applying it as gradient weighting $`r_{t}`$
for each training token $`y_{t}`$ in a trajectory
$`y=\{y_{t}\}_{t<|y|}`$. This leads to our final reweighting ratio:
$`r_{t}=\sigma\left(\tau\log\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x;y_{:<t})}{\bar{\pi}_{T}(y_{t}\mid x;c;y_{:<t})}\right).`$

This formulation can be readily applied to different offline
distillation backbones. We illustrate with SFT as the base objective:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nabla_{\theta}J^{\text{{DisCorD} }}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{Q},\;y\sim\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x;c)}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{|y|}\sigma(\tau\log\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x;y_{:<t})}{\bar{\pi_{T}}(y_{t}\mid x;c;y_{:<t})})\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x;y_{:<t})\right].
``` |  | (5) |

We refer to the proposed framework as DisCorD (Distribution-Corrected
Distillation), which modulates the influence of teacher-provided data
supervision based on the student’s current support. It is also
compatible with other offline distillation objectives beyond SFT, such
as the KL-based formulation in
Eq. ([4](#S2.E4 "In Offline Knowledge Distillation. ‣ 2 Preliminary ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"))
by replacing the gradient of SFT with that of KL minimization
(Section [5](#S5 "5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")).

#### Implications of the Token-Level Correction.

The correction weight at token $`t`$ takes the form using a default
temperature of 1:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle r_{t}|_{\tau=1}=\sigma\!\left(\log\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x;y_{:<t})}{\bar{\pi}_{T}(y_{t}\mid x;c;y_{:<t})}\right)=\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x;y_{:<t})}{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x;y_{:<t})+\bar{\pi}_{T}(y_{t}\mid x;c;y_{:<t})}.`$ |  |

It can be interpreted as the posterior probability that token $`y_{t}`$
was drawn from the student distribution $`\pi_{\theta}`$ over the
teacher distribution $`\pi_{T}`$, under a uniform prior over the two
models \[[10](#bib.bib10)\]. This also connects to contrastive
decoding \[[19](#bib.bib19)\], which was applied at model inference time
by amplifying the target model’s log-probabilities relative to a weaker
model. In contrast, our formulation applies an analogous principle
during training, which uses the student-teacher ratio as a soft
reweighting to prioritize learning in regions the student is likely to
inhabit at inference time.

We demonstrate in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")
that this distribution correction improves distilled model performance
beyond the instruction prompting baseline with a carefully designed
reasoning template. In contrast, several baseline distillation methods
can underperform the base model that is prompted with the same reasoning
instruction but without fine-tuning.

## 4 Related Work

We study offline LLM reasoning distillation that tackles the
teacher-student distribution drift on fixed offline training traces.
This work resides at the intersection of knowledge distillation,
post-training optimization, and mathematical reasoning supervision.

#### Knowledge Distillation (KD).

Knowledge Distillation was initially proposed for conventional AI
models, in which a compact student model learns from a stronger teacher
via softened predictive distributions or intermediate representations
 \[[3](#bib.bib3), [2](#bib.bib2), [13](#bib.bib13), [27](#bib.bib27)\].
This paradigm has been extended to LLMs, where intermediate rationales
beyond final answers can be distilled from a strong teacher to a smaller
student  \[[28](#bib.bib28), [16](#bib.bib16), [14](#bib.bib14),
[15](#bib.bib15)\]. Early reasoning-distillation studies such as
Fine-tune-CoT \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] and Distilling
Step-by-Step \[[15](#bib.bib15)\] established the value of
teacher-generated rationales as supervision for smaller models.
Subsequent work has studied how the quality, format, and composition of
teacher traces affect distillation. Other studies have improved
teacher-generated traces through rationale selection, filtering,
structured explanations, and math-specific data
curation \[[38](#bib.bib38), [35](#bib.bib35), [23](#bib.bib23),
[22](#bib.bib22), [44](#bib.bib44), [33](#bib.bib33), [5](#bib.bib5)\].
These works motivated the use of high-quality offline teacher-generated
reasoning traces. However, most methods still train the student model by
imitating fixed teacher trajectories under teacher-conditioned prefix
distributions. They therefore leave the training-inference distribution
drift relatively underexplored: the student is optimized under teacher
prefixes during training, but autoregresses on its own prefixes during
inference \[[1](#bib.bib1), [9](#bib.bib9), [18](#bib.bib18),
[17](#bib.bib17)\].

#### LLM Post-Training with On-policy vs. Offline Data.

A closer line of work tackles this distribution shift more directly:
Online RL and other self-improvement methods optimize on model-generated
trajectories over fixed teacher traces. PPO-style RLHF
methods \[[29](#bib.bib29), [25](#bib.bib25)\] and recent
reasoning-oriented RL methods such as GRPO \[[30](#bib.bib30),
[7](#bib.bib7)\] generate rollouts from the target model and update the
model using outcome or process rewards. Related online or mixed-policy
distillation methods, including GKD \[[1](#bib.bib1)\] and
CoTD-PO \[[24](#bib.bib24)\], also use student-conditioned or
iteratively generated trajectories to better match inference-time
behavior. These methods directly reduce the gap between training and
inference distributions, but they require additional online sampling,
substantially more training-time tokens, and often encounter low-quality
student-generated traces early in training. A complementary line of work
focuses on redesigning the distillation directions.
MiniLLM \[[9](#bib.bib9)\], DistiLLM \[[18](#bib.bib18)\], and
ToDi \[[17](#bib.bib17)\] modify autoregressive knowledge-distillation
losses through reverse KL, skewed KL, or token-wise divergence control,
to better align training and generation behavior. Methods such as
DistiLLM still require online student sampling to minimize the reverse
KL divergence. Our method resides in the purely offline setting, but
focuses on the correction at a different level: instead of changing the
divergence measure, we adaptively reweight teacher-token supervision
based on the student–teacher distribution mismatch. In this sense, our
method changes how the offline teacher supervision is allocated, thus
producing a distribution-corrected training signal while preserving the
sample efficiency of fixed teacher traces. Our formulation can be
readily combined with SFT and other KL-based divergence measures.
Compared with online methods such as GKD and CoTD-PO, our method remains
fully offline without requiring student rollouts. Prior offline
distillation work, such as ToDi, has mainly been applied to the
instruction-following domain; we studied DisCorD’s effect in
mathematical reasoning distillation as an empirically more challenging
domain
(Sec [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Reasoning Accuracy Comparison ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")).

#### Math Reasoning Supervision and Evaluation.

Mathematical reasoning also motivates fine-grained supervision: uniform
imitation treats all teacher tokens equally, even though an early
algebraic or logical error can propagate through an entire solution.
This has motivated process-level supervision and verifier-style
frameworks. Outcome-level verifiers and reward models judge complete
solutions or final answers \[[6](#bib.bib6), [31](#bib.bib31)\], while
process-supervised methods provide finer-grained feedback on
intermediate reasoning steps \[[34](#bib.bib34), [20](#bib.bib20),
[36](#bib.bib36)\]. Related correction-based frameworks further use
teacher feedback to identify and revise erroneous reasoning
traces \[[41](#bib.bib41)\].

Our work is complementary to this literature: we design a
chain-of-thought reasoning template to elicit strong reasoning traces
from the teacher model without introducing a new verifier or search
procedure. We then move beyond uniform token imitation and use
mismatch-aware reweighting to emphasize teacher supervision that better
aligns with the student-conditioned inference distribution.

## 5 Experiments

We evaluate our method on mathematical reasoning benchmarks across
diverse teacher-student configurations, varying model families, sizes,
and tasks, with both in- and out-of-domain assessment and qualitative
trace analysis. We provide additional results on more experimental
settings in the
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Training and Evaluation Audit Details ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models").
Our main experiments were organized around four questions:

Q1. Does our offline distillation method improve the student model’s
reasoning compared to state-of-the-art offline distillation counterparts
(Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Reasoning Accuracy Comparison ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"))?

Q2. Is the distillation benefit consistent across different model
families
(Section [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Robustness Across Model Distillation Settings ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"))?

Q3. Does the method actually reduce teacher-student behavior divergence
under student-generated prefixes during inference time
(Section [5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Distribution Divergence Measurement ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"))?

Q4. Does the resulting student reasoning performance reflect higher
quality in correctness, conciseness, and reliability
(Section [5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 Reasoning Quality Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"))?

Q5. Why do we adopt the proposed transformations for stabilizing the
distribution correction weights instead of alternative formulations
(Section [5.6](#S5.SS6 "5.6 Comparing Alternative Correction-Weight Designs ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"))?

### 5.1 Experimental Setup: Baselines, Metrics, and Evaluation Protocols

#### Models and Teacher Reasoning Instruction.

We used Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct as
teachers \[[26](#bib.bib26)\], with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct,
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, and Llama-3.2-3B as students. Teacher traces were
generated offline using a structured reasoning prompt
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Teacher Chain-of-Thought Prompt ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"))
that elicits five stages: problem understanding, strategy selection,
solution, verification, and final answer. We retained only traces where
the teacher’s final answer is correct for distillation training. The
same generation-and-filtering pipeline was used for both MATH and GSM8K
training data.

#### Benchmarks.

For in-domain evaluation, we distill on MATH \[[12](#bib.bib12)\] and
GSM8K \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] training splits and evaluate on their
corresponding test sets, e.g., using MATH500 \[[20](#bib.bib20)\] for
MATH-trained checkpoints. For out-of-domain (OOD) evaluation, models
trained on MATH were further tested on
OlympiadBench \[[11](#bib.bib11)\]²² 2 For OlympiadBench, we evaluated
all performance on the non-combinatorics subset as all training corpora
contain no combinatorics problems., Omni-Math \[[8](#bib.bib8)\], and
AMC23, which do not appear in the training domain.

#### Baselines.

We compared both fully offline distillation objectives and an online
baseline. SFT uses the basic cross-entropy loss on teacher-generated
reasoning traces. KL uses KL divergence to measure teacher-student
distribution difference on the same offline traces, symmetric KL
combines forward KL and reverse KL divergence terms, following the
broader line of LLM distillation work that studies forward/reverse KL
combinations and bidirectional divergence objectives \[[17](#bib.bib17),
[40](#bib.bib40)\]. ToDi \[[17](#bib.bib17)\] is an offline distillation
baseline. GKD \[[1](#bib.bib1)\] is an online method reported for
reference that relies on frequent sampling of student-generated traces
for training. For objectives where our correction is applicable,
including SFT and KL, the DisCorD-augmented variant applies the proposed
token-level reweighting to the same fixed teacher traces. See Appendix
[G](#A7 "Appendix G DisCorD Applied to KL Distillation Objective ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")
for detailed formulation. We also report the base model, the
CoT-prompted student, and the CoT-prompted teacher as reference points
for interpreting lower-bound, prompting-only, and teacher-level
performance.

#### Evaluation metrics.

Final-answer accuracy ($`\uparrow`$) is our primary metric computed
using a mathematical-equivalence pipeline. Distributional ExAccErr
$`\downarrow`$: For divergence measurement, we evaluated the additional
teacher-student next-token distribution gap induced by conditioning on
student-generated prefixes rather than teacher prefixes. The initial
definition was proposed in MiniLLM \[[9](#bib.bib9)\].
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Definition of ExAccErr Metric ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")
provides the detailed formulation. Reasoning reliability: In Section
[5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 Reasoning Quality Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"),
we evaluated whether correct answers produced by our method are
supported by stable reasoning quality using both automatic metrics and
AI-as-Judge annotations. See
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Training and Evaluation Audit Details ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")
for more details.

### 5.2 Reasoning Accuracy Comparison

This subsection evaluates final-answer accuracy along two axes: (i)
whether DisCorD improves fully offline teacher-trace distillation
compared with prior art, and (ii) how offline distillation methods
compare with online training with student-rollouts such as GKD, and how
they compare with tuning-free methods using a carefully designed
reasoning instruction. The results lead to three main observations:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | In-Domain Performance |  | Out of Domain Performance |  |  |
| Model / method | MATH500 | GSM8K | OlympiadBench | Omni-Math | AMC23 |
| Reference models |  |  |  |  |  |
| Qwen2.5-3B (base) | 42.60 | 55.19 | 25.19 | 17.50 | 32.50 |
| Qwen2.5-3B w/ CoT Instruct | 60.20 | 81.12 | 29.81 | 28.50 | 35.00 |
| Qwen2.5-7B | 55.80 | 69.07 | 34.04 | 27.00 | 35.00 |
| Qwen2.5-7B w/ CoT Instruct (teacher) | 69.40 | 88.78 | 39.04 | 36.50 | 45.00 |
| GKD (online distillation) | 62.80 | 83.62 | 33.00 | 32.00 | 35.00 |
| Offline distilled methods |  |  |  |  |  |
| SFT | 58.00 | 83.47 | 31.00 | 26.50 | 32.50 |
| SFT w/ DisCorD | 62.60 ($`\uparrow`$4.60) | 83.02 ($`\downarrow`$0.45) | 31.70 ($`\uparrow`$0.70) | 29.50 ($`\uparrow`$3.00) | 40.00 ($`\uparrow`$7.50) |
| ToDi | 59.20 | 83.09 | 31.20 | 28.00 | 37.50 |
| KL | 59.00 | 83.93 | 30.00 | 26.00 | 32.50 |
| Symmetric KL | 59.20 | 83.55 | 28.65 | 28.50 | 37.50 |
| Symmetric KL w/ DisCorD | 61.80 ($`\uparrow`$2.60) | 83.55 ($`\pm`$0.00) | 30.38 ($`\uparrow`$1.73) | 29.00 ($`\uparrow`$0.50) | 37.50 ($`\pm`$0.00) |

Table 1: Distillation from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct $`\rightarrow`$
Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. DisCorD generally improves over offline baselines
on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks, while also outperforming the
training-free instruction-prompting approach. "w/ CoT Instruct" denotes
model performance instructed by our proposed reasoning template without
training. All entries are accuracy (%). Parenthesized metrics indicate
performance changes introduced by DisCorD relative to the corresponding
base objective, where available.

First, DisCorD yields the most consistent gains on MATH-style reasoning
tasks, where solutions typically require longer reasoning traces and
prefix drift is more likely to affect generation. As shown in Table
[1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Reasoning Accuracy Comparison ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"),
on the in-domain MATH500 benchmark, DisCorD improves the corresponding
offline objectives in the main Qwen settings. The gains are not limited
to standard teacher-CoT SFT: our method also improves the symmetric-KL
objective in multiple settings, suggesting that the proposed correction
can serve as a flexible reweighting mechanism for different offline
distillation losses.

Comparisons with tuning-free prompting further highlight this effect. In
the 7B$`\rightarrow`$3B setting, SFT underperforms the
instruction-prompted student on MATH500, while DisCorD achieves
performance beyond instruction prompting. This indicates that direct
behavior cloning on teacher traces may weaken the student’s potential
for reasoning elicitation, whereas our method allocates supervision more
effectively to teacher tokens that remain compatible with the student’s
own generation behavior.

Results on GSM8K are less discriminative, likely because the task
requires shorter reasoning traces and is less impacted by prefix
distribution drift. Strong baselines already plateau after training on
traces generated by our reasoning instruction. For example, in the
7B$`\rightarrow`$3B setting, SFT+DisCorD is slightly below SFT on GSM8K,
and symmetric KL+DisCorD is tied with symmetric KL, even though DisCorD
improves the corresponding MATH500 results and several OOD benchmarks.
We consider GSM8K as a shorter-trace setting where the benefit of
distribution correction is less pronounced. This interpretation is
consistent with our ablations in
Section [5.6](#S5.SS6 "5.6 Comparing Alternative Correction-Weight Designs ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")
and Appendix
[A](#A1 "Appendix A DisCorD Temperature Tuning ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"),
where different transformations of the correction weight have more
pronounced effects on longer MATH-style tasks, whereas GSM8K is less
sensitive to a specific correction-weighting design.

Second, the improvements transfer to OOD competition-style benchmarks.
In the 7B$`\rightarrow`$3B setting, DisCorD outperforms the
corresponding offline objectives on several OOD evaluations, including
OlympiadBench, Omni-Math, and AMC23. These results suggest that
distribution-corrected distillation improves generalization to related
competition-style mathematical reasoning tasks.

Third, our method narrows the gap to online student-rollout
distillation. GKD remains stronger on some in-domain and OOD benchmarks,
as expected, because it trains on student-conditioned online samples and
directly observes the student’s rollout distribution. In contrast,
DisCorD uses only fixed teacher traces, yet achieves stronger
performance than offline baselines. Concretely, DisCorD generates no
student-rollout tokens during training and uses only 3.12 GPU-hours,
while GKD generates about 2.86M online student-rollout tokens and
requires 49.56 GPU-hours, about 15.9$`\times`$ more compute. This
suggests that our distribution-corrected distillation can approach the
benefits of online training while preserving the sample efficiency of
offline learning.

DisCorD consistently improves offline baselines across model families.

We further examined the robustness of different methods under varying
teacher-student size configurations and model families.
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Reasoning Accuracy Comparison ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")
reports results using Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct as the teacher and
Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct as the student, which are
consistent with the main findings: our distribution correction method
generally improves offline distillation objectives across both student
sizes, and is most beneficial for longer mathematical reasoning traces,
where teacher-student prefix mismatch has more room to affect
generation. For the 14B$`\rightarrow`$3B setting, SFT+DisCorD improves
over SFT on both MATH500 and GSM8K, with gains of 2.20 and 1.52 points,
respectively. For the smaller 14B$`\rightarrow`$1.5B setting, the gains
are larger on MATH500.

To isolate the effect of the student model family, we also distilled a
Llama-3.2-3B student from Qwen2.5 teachers using the same objectives as
in the main experiments, and evaluated the resulting models on MATH500.
As shown in
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Robustness Across Model Distillation Settings ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"),
the cross-family results are consistent with the primary findings in
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Reasoning Accuracy Comparison ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"):
the DisCorD-augmented objectives remain competitive with baselines that
minimize teacher-student logit divergence and outperform the untuned
base model with CoT instructions. In both teacher settings, SFT+DisCorD
is the strongest distilled method, which improves over SFT by 3.0 and
2.0 points, respectively. Consistent with
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Reasoning Accuracy Comparison ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"),
adding DisCorD also improves the symmetric-KL objective in both
settings. These results suggest that the proposed mismatch-aware
reweighting remains effective across different distillation settings.

### 5.4 Distribution Divergence Measurement

To evaluate reasoning robustness under student-generated prefixes, we
sampled prefixes from the base student before training instead of from
teacher traces. Specifically, we randomly sampled 200 MATH test problems
and let the base student model generate partial solutions. From each
partial solution, we truncated prefix horizons with
$`t\in\{32,64,128,256\}`$ tokens.
Figure [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5.4 Distribution Divergence Measurement ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")
reports ExAccErr ($`\downarrow`$) for SFT and our method, where lower
values indicate smaller divergence between the student model’s
continuation answers and the expected answer distribution under the
given prefixes. Specifically, each continuation answer is sampled from
the trained student model conditioned on a provided prefix.

Figure 2: Comparing policy divergence (ExAccErr): A base model provides
reasoning prefixes truncated at length $`t\in\{32,64,128,256\}`$. Lower
ExAccErr indicates less divergence in continuation behavior under
student-generated prefixes. DisCorD remains more robust to prefix drift
than SFT as prefix length increases.

As the prefix horizon $`t`$ increases, SFT exhibits a notably growing
ExAccErr, which indicates that its behavior becomes increasingly
unstable when conditioned on longer student-generated reasoning
prefixes. In contrast, DisCorD keeps ExAccErr stable across prefix
lengths. This indicates that our proposed distribution correction
improves robustness to prefix drift and reduces the amplification of
errors introduced by student-generated intermediate reasoning. Overall,
this result shows that the benefit of DisCorD is not limited to
final-answer accuracy. By reducing sensitivity to long student-generated
prefixes, it better preserves reliable continuation behavior within
support regions likely to be visited by student models.

### 5.5 Reasoning Quality Analysis

In addition to the improved final-answer accuracy and reduced
teacher-student distribution drift as shown above, we examined whether
performance gains of our method manifest in the generated reasoning
traces themselves. In particular, we investigated whether the correct
answers are supported by more logically coherent and stable reasoning
traces, and whether reducing the distribution drift in training
alleviates typical generation failures such as repetition, post-answer
continuation (i.e., non-stop generation after providing a final answer),
and inconsistent final answers (i.e., providing multiple distinct
answers). For fair comparisons, we focused primarily on commonly-correct
examples where both SFT and DisCorD produce the correct final answer.

|-------------------------------|---------------|---------|--------|---------|
|  Metric                       | SFT           | DisCorD | SFT    | DisCorD |
|  Mean len. $`\downarrow`$     | 5328.1        | 1651.0  | 4383.0 | 1357.9  |
|  Rep. 4-gram $`\downarrow`$   | 0.5603        | 0.3288  | 0.6514 | 0.2698  |
|  Post-answer $`\downarrow`$   | 0.6000        | 0.1000  | 0.7900 | 0.1500  |
|  Multi-answer $`\downarrow`$  | 0.5900        | 0.0000  | 0.7500 | 0.0000  |

Table 4: Comparing reasoning-trace quality between SFT and DisCorD.
Lower values indicate more desirable traces.

#### Reasoning Trace Pattern Quality.

To examine whether our method improves generation patterns, we compared
DisCorD with the SFT baseline using four automatic trace-quality
metrics: mean trace length in characters (Mean len), the fraction of
repeated 4-grams in the generated trace (Rep. 4-gram), the rate of
continuing generation after emitting a final answer (Post-answer), and
the rate of producing multiple distinct final-answer statements within
the same trace (Multi-answer). As shown in
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.5 Reasoning Quality Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"),
on MATH, our method decreases the mean trace length from 4383.0 to
1357.9 characters and the multiple-answer rate from 0.75 to 0, while
also substantially lowering repetition and post-answer continuation
rates. A similar pattern also appears on OlympiadBench. Beyond improving
final-answer accuracy, even within the commonly correct subset, DisCorD
yields cleaner generation patterns by producing shorter traces with
fewer repetitions, post-answer continuations, and multiple-answer
failures.

#### Evaluation of Reasoning Trace Quality.

Figure 3: Comparing reasoning trace quality.

To complement the automatic metrics above, we further evaluated the
generated traces using GPT-5.4 mini as a judge with a predefined rubric.
The rubric covers five dimensions: cleanliness, validity (i.e., whether
the reasoning is valid when the answer is correct), self-consistency,
reasoning quality, and verification quality.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Evaluation Details and Correctness Judge ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")
provides the definitions of each metric, the scoring protocol, and the
full results. As shown in
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Evaluation of Reasoning Trace Quality. ‣ 5.5 Reasoning Quality Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"),
these AI-as-judge annotation results are consistent with the evaluation
using automatic metrics in Table
[4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.5 Reasoning Quality Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models").
Crucially, this suggests that the shorter responses produced by DisCorD
are not merely more concise but also more logically coherent and
internally consistent. The detailed results further show that DisCorD
reduces the fraction of traces with a correct final answer but flawed
reasoning from 26% to 11% on OlympiadBench and from 20% to 7% on MATH.
In addition, DisCorD receives higher reasoning and verification quality
scores. These results together indicate a qualitative improvement in the
reasoning traces underlying the final-answer accuracy gains.

#### Reasoning Trace Case Study.

We further analyzed representative examples from one in-domain dataset,
MATH, and one out-of-domain dataset, OlympiadBench. A concise case
summary and representative trace analyses are provided in
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Reasoning Trace Case Study ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models").
The examples illustrate two qualitative patterns. (1) First, in
failure-recovery cases, where DisCorD answers correctly while the SFT
baseline fails (example A–D), our method more reliably preserves the
underlying reasoning structure of the teacher solution, even when it
does not exactly reproduce the teacher’s surface-level formatting, such
as the section headers: “PLAN”, “VERIFICATION”, etc. Specifically, in
the OlympiadBench divisor-counting problem, DisCorD does not verbatim
reproduce the teacher’s verification section titled "VEriFICATION", but
it keeps the teacher’s core logic by using the correct factorization and
checks the resulting answer consistently. In contrast, the SFT baseline
follows the expected template more closely, but its verification step
uses an incorrect factorization and counting argument that leads to the
wrong answer. (2) Second, in overlap-correct cases (example E–H), where
both models reach the correct final answer, DisCorD often produces a
cleaner and more direct solution, with fewer unnecessary branches and
more relevant checks. These observations are consistent with the
aforementioned metrics: DisCorD can improve reasoning trace reliability
by preserving core reasoning content instead of verbatim imitating the
teacher’s formatting.

Overall, our qualitative studies indicate that DisCorD improves
reasoning trace reliability beyond final-answer accuracy. On commonly
correct examples, our method yields cleaner and more logically stable
traces; in failure-recovery cases, it more often preserves the
mathematical structure needed to reach the correct answer. These
findings imply that student-support-aware distribution correction
strengthens offline reasoning distillation not by enforcing
surface-level template imitation, but by reallocating teacher
supervision toward reasoning behaviors that the student can more
reliably carry through at inference time.

Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.6 Comparing Alternative Correction-Weight Designs ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")
compares several correction-weight designs under the same prompt and

against clipped exponential weighting, the raw log-ratio, and a
one-sided ReLU transform. Our formulation achieves the strongest result
among the tested variants and inherits a theoretical interpretation
grounded in noise-contrastive estimation.

## 6 Conclusion and Future Work

We propose a simple yet effective offline distillation method for
mitigating teacher–student distribution drift in tasks requiring long
reasoning traces. Our method keeps the training data fully offline but
reweights teacher-token supervision based on a student–teacher support
ratio, thereby prioritizing teacher behaviors that are more compatible
with the student’s inference-time distribution. Comprehensive evaluation
on mathematical reasoning benchmarks shows that our method improves
final-answer accuracy over strong offline baselines, narrows the gap to
online student-rollout distillation, and yields more logical and
higher-quality reasoning traces. While our experiments focus on
mathematical reasoning, the proposed method can be extended to other
long-horizon generation settings, including code generation, scientific
reasoning, and tool-use agents. Future work may include integrating our
method with off-policy or online training to better balance data
efficiency and distillation efficacy. Another future direction is to
decouple teacher trace generation from distribution correction scoring:
when a trace-generating teacher is unavailable or unknown, a proxy
reference model—potentially a weaker one—or an arbitrary policy may be
used to approximate the support-ratio weights. This may preserve the
core benefit of prioritizing student-reachable tokens while offering
greater flexibility in the trade-off between teacher data quality and
robustness to training-inference distribution shift.

## Appendix A DisCorD Temperature Tuning

Table [A](#A1 "Appendix A DisCorD Temperature Tuning ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")
reports the sigmoid temperatures used for the DisCORD-augmented rows in
the main result tables. We tune this temperature within each
teacher–student setting and base objective, rather than using a single
global value across all experiments. This is because the scale of the
student–teacher log-probability gap can change with teacher size,
student capacity, dataset, and whether DisCORD is applied on top of SFT
or symmetric KL. For MATH-trained checkpoints, the same temperature is
used for the MATH500 in-domain evaluation and for the OOD evaluations,
since the OOD benchmarks reuse the MATH-trained models. GSM8K results
are listed separately because they come from independently trained GSM8K
checkpoints.

## Appendix B Teacher Chain-of-Thought Prompt

We designed this teacher CoT prompt ourselves to elicit structured,
self-verifying reasoning with explicit understanding, strategy,
solution, and verification stages. Following established prompt design
principles such as role specification, explicit output structure, and
self-consistency checks \[[39](#bib.bib39), [37](#bib.bib37)\], we
refined the template on a held-out sample of training questions and did
not tune the prompt against the evaluation benchmarks.

## Appendix C Training and Evaluation Audit Details

This section collects the implementation details used to make the
experimental comparisons auditable. The main comparison is
objective-level: within each teacher–student–dataset setting, all
offline objectives are trained on the same retained teacher-generated
trace corpus and differ only in the loss or token weighting applied to
that corpus.

#### Training corpus construction.

For MATH-family experiments, teacher traces are generated from the MATH
training split ($`7{,}500`$ source problems). For GSM8K experiments,
teacher traces are generated from the GSM8K training split ($`7{,}473`$
source problems). Each source problem is prompted once with the
structured teacher prompt in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Teacher Chain-of-Thought Prompt ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models");
the generated trace is then filtered by the same final-answer
equivalence judge used in evaluation. We retain only teacher-correct
traces for distillation. The retained subset, retained count, and
average teacher-trace length are fixed before student training and are
shared by all offline objectives within the corresponding
teacher–student setting. Cross-family Llama experiments reuse the same
Qwen2.5 teacher-trace construction pipeline as the Qwen-student
experiments.

#### Offline Training Protocol and hyperparameters.

Within a teacher–student setting and data split, the fully offline
methods (SFT, KL, symmetric KL, ToDi, and DisCorD-augmented variants)
are trained on the same retained teacher-correct examples and use the
same offline training recipe: AdamW with learning rate
$`3\times 10^{-6}`$, weight decay $`0.01`$, cosine decay with $`5\%`$
warmup, gradient clipping at norm $`1.0`$, bfloat16 mixed precision,
maximum sequence length 2048, random seed 42, and effective batch size
16. For MATH-family runs, this corresponds to micro-batch size 1 with
gradient accumulation 16; for GSM8K, micro-batch size 2 with gradient
accumulation 8. The number of epochs is fixed within each matched
setting and base objective, so changes in
Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Reasoning Accuracy Comparison ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"),
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Reasoning Accuracy Comparison ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"),
and
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Robustness Across Model Distillation Settings ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")
are not attributable to different amounts of offline teacher data or
different offline training-token budgets. Hyperparameters that define an
objective itself, such as the KL/ToDi temperature or the sigmoid
temperature for DisCorD, are selected per setting and base objective and
are reported in the corresponding table captions or rows when they
differ.

#### Online Protocol and hyperparameters.

GKD is reported separately because it is not a compute-matched offline
baseline. It uses student rollouts during training and follows its own
on-policy recipe: AdamW with learning rate $`3\times 10^{-6}`$, weight
decay $`0.01`$, cosine decay with $`5\%`$ warmup, gradient clipping at
norm $`1.0`$, maximum sequence length 2048, effective batch size 16,
$`\beta=0.5`$ following the original paper setting, and one training
epoch in the reported runs, with the on-policy mixing parameter
$`\lambda`$ specified by the corresponding run. We therefore treat GKD
as an online reference rather than as evidence about the matched offline
training-token budget.

#### Evaluation protocol.

All methods in a setting use the same evaluation prompt, greedy decoding
protocol, and maximum generation length. The generation caps are 2048
new tokens for GSM8K, MATH500, and 4096 new tokens for AMC23, Omni-Math
and OlympiadBench. Final-answer correctness is judged by GPT-5.4-mini
using the same mathematical-equivalence prompt for every method. The
judge is not given the method identity and is instructed to ignore
reasoning quality and compare only the final answer. If a solution
contains multiple candidate answers, the judge follows the explicitly
marked final answer, such as one introduced by “final”, “answer”,
“therefore”, or `\boxed{}`. The full judge prompt appears in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Evaluation Details and Correctness Judge ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models").

#### Compute resources.

Experiments were run on SLURM-managed GPU clusters. Unless otherwise
noted, training and evaluation jobs used NVIDIA A100 40GB GPUs;
GPU-hours are reported as the number of allocated GPUs multiplied by
wall-clock runtime. In the main 7B$`\rightarrow`$3B comparison, the
DisCorD run uses no online student-rollout tokens and requires 3.12
GPU-hours, whereas the GKD online baseline generates about 2.86M
student-rollout tokens and requires 49.56 GPU-hours. The reported
GPU-hour comparison covers training compute for the matched distillation
setting; teacher-trace generation, benchmark evaluation, and
GPT-5.4-mini judge calls are one-time preprocessing or evaluation costs
shared across methods within each setting.

## Appendix D Evaluation Details and Correctness Judge

Main in-domain evaluation uses MATH500 \[[20](#bib.bib20)\] for
MATH-trained checkpoints ($`n=500`$) and GSM8K \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] for
GSM8K-trained checkpoints ($`n=1{,}319`$). OOD evaluation uses the
non-combinatorics portion of OlympiadBench OE_TO_maths_en_COMP
($`n=520`$ after removing combinatorics problems), the fixed Omni-Math
D3/D4 paper subset \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] ($`n=200`$), and AMC23 ($`n=40`$).
We exclude OlympiadBench combinatorics problems because the MATH
teacher-trace training corpus used here contains no combinatorics
examples.

All distilled checkpoints are evaluated with the same finetuning-style
prompt template and greedy decoding. We use generation caps of 2048 new
tokens for GSM8K, MATH500, and AMC23, and 4096 new tokens for Omni-Math
and OlympiadBench.

We judge final-answer correctness with GPT-5.4-mini. The judge is
instructed to ignore reasoning quality and compare only the final answer
by mathematical equivalence. The prompt template is as below:

## Appendix G DisCorD Applied to KL Distillation Objective

For KL-based offline distillation, we apply the same token-level sigmoid
correction used in
Eq. ([5](#S3.E5 "In Stabilized Transformation. ‣ 3 Methodology: Distribution Corrected Distillation from Offline Data ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models"))
to the teacher–student next-token divergence. The corresponding loss is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{KL}+\textsc{DisCorD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{Q},\;y\sim\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x;c)}\left[\sum_{t}r_{t}\,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\bar{\pi}_{T}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t};c)\,\middle\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\right)\right],
``` |  | (6) |

where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{t}=\sigma\!\left(\tau\log\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{\bar{\pi}_{T}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t};c)}\right).
``` |  | (7) |

Here $`\bar{\pi}`$ denotes a stop-gradient distribution and $`\tau`$ is
the sigmoid temperature.

## Appendix H Definition of ExAccErr Metric

We follow the original MiniLLM-style ExAccErr definition. For an input
question $`x`$, let $`y^{T}=(y^{T}_{1},\ldots,y^{T}_{T})`$ denote the
teacher CoT rollout and let $`y^{m}=(y^{m}_{1},\ldots,y^{m}_{T_{m}})`$
denote the rollout of method $`m\in\{\text{SFT},\text{Ours}\}`$. At step
$`t`$, given a prefix $`z_{<t}`$, we define the teacher–student
next-token gap as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
d_{t}^{m}(z_{<t})=\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{T}(\cdot\mid x,z_{<t})\,\|\,q_{m}(\cdot\mid x,z_{<t})\right),
``` |  |

where $`p_{T}`$ and $`q_{m}`$ are the teacher and method-$`m`$ student
next-token distributions, respectively. We then accumulate this gap
under teacher prefixes and under method-$`m`$ student prefixes:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
E_{\mathrm{teacher}}^{m}(\ell)=\sum_{t=1}^{\ell}d_{t}^{m}(y^{T}_{<t}),\qquad E_{\mathrm{student}}^{m}(\ell)=\sum_{t=1}^{\ell}d_{t}^{m}(y^{m}_{<t}),
``` |  |

and define

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{ExAccErr}^{m}(\ell)=\frac{E_{\mathrm{student}}^{m}(\ell)-E_{\mathrm{teacher}}^{m}(\ell)}{E_{\mathrm{teacher}}^{m}(\ell)}\times 100\%.
``` |  |

Lower metrics are desirable.

## Appendix I Reasoning Trace Case Study

Table [I](#A9 "Appendix I Reasoning Trace Case Study ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models")
summarizes the eight qualitative examples discussed in
Section [5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 Reasoning Quality Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Distribution Corrected Offline Data Distillation for Large Language Models").
Examples A–D are failure-recovery cases, where DisCorD reaches the
correct final answer while the SFT baseline fails. Examples E–H are
overlap-correct cases, where both student models answer correctly and
the comparison focuses on trace quality. To keep the appendix concise,
we summarize all eight cases and reproduce the original raw traces for
two representative cases only.

| Case | Dataset | ID | Type |  Main contrast |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| A | MATH | 108 | Recovery |  Ratio algebra: DisCorD uses $`y=2x`$ and verifies the substitution; SFT reverses the ratio relation and solves the wrong equation. |
| B | MATH | 705 | Recovery |  Finite braking sequence: DisCorD sums the arithmetic sequence to 225; SFT introduces an irrelevant geometric-series framing before reaching an unstable solution. |
| C | OlyBench | 2438 | Recovery |  Functional equation: DisCorD follows the direct chain $`0\mapsto 3\mapsto 9`$; SFT recurses through unknown values such as $`f(1)`$ and outputs 69. |
| D | OlyBench | 2776 | Recovery |  Divisor count: DisCorD preserves the teacher’s factorization $`K=(2T+1)(T+1)^{2}=43\cdot 22^{2}`$; SFT mis-factors $`K`$ and selects 743. |
| E | MATH | 2041 | Both correct |  Both solve the right-triangle problem; DisCorD uses the complementary-angle identity more directly, while SFT is more template-heavy. |
| F | MATH | 640 | Both correct |  Both derive $`h^{-1}(5)=3/2`$; DisCorD stops after one clean derivation, while SFT repeats the same solution block after the final answer. |
| G | OlyBench | 2785 | Both correct |  Both compute the units digit correctly; DisCorD gives a compact modular-cycle argument, while SFT appends an unnecessary code-style verification. |
| H | OlyBench | 2441 | Both correct |  Both students apply inclusion–exclusion correctly; DisCorD is shorter and avoids repeated counting steps. |

Table 9: Summary of qualitative reasoning-trace cases.

EXAMPLE E DATASET: MATH Analysis. The problem asks for the greatest
prime factor of the divisor count of $`20^{T}23^{T}`$ with $`T=21`$. The
teacher’s core solution is $`20^{T}23^{T}=2^{2T}5^{T}23^{T}`$ and
$`K=(2T+1)(T+1)^{2}=43\cdot 22^{2}`$. DisCorD preserves this
divisor-count factorization and identifies 43. SFT follows the surface
template more closely, but its verification incorrectly factors
$`20812`$ as $`2^{2}\cdot 7\cdot 743`$ and therefore changes the answer
to 743. This shows that DisCorD need not copy the teacher’s headings to
retain the mathematical structure that matters.
````
